label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
For all sufficiently large $n$, if $P$ is a partial Latin square and $L$ is a
Latin square of order $n$, then there are permutations
$\pi,\sigma\in\mathcal S_n$ such that
\[\sigma\bigl(L(\pi(i),j)\bigr)\ne P(i,j)
\]
for every filled cell $(i,j)$ of $P$.
head: environment

label: thm:ACM
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ACM}
There are positive constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that the following is true for every positive integer $n$. Suppose that $P$ is a partial Latin square of order $n$ in which each row and column has at most $\alpha n$ non-empty cells. 
Suppose that $A$ is an $n\times n$ array of subsets of $[n]$, each of size at most $\beta n$, in which
each symbol occurs at most $\beta n$ times among the sets in each row and column. Then if no cell of $P$ contains a symbol that occurs in the corresponding cell of $A$, then there is a completion of $P$ that avoids $A$.

label: lem:hit
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hit}
Fix $r$.  Let $M_1,\dots,M_r$ be pairwise edge-disjoint matchings in $K_{n,n}$, and let $\Pi$ be a uniformly random perfect matching.
Then, uniformly in the choice of the $M_i$,
\[
 \Pr\big(\Pi\cap M_i\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }i\in[r]\big)
   \leqslant\bigl(1-\mathrm e^{-1}\bigr)^r+o(1).
\]
head: environment

label: eq:rook
title: Proof
body_md:
For $J\subseteq[r]$, put $F_J=\bigcup_{j\in J}M_j$.  Suppose that the graph $F_J$ has $m\leqslant|J|n$ edges, and note that its maximum degree is at most $r$.  Let $q_k(F_J)$ be the number of $k$-edge matchings contained in $F_J$. For each fixed $k$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rook}
 q_k(F_J)                                
 = \frac{m^k}{k!}-O_{r,k}(n^{k-1}).
\end{equation}
Indeed, start with all $k$-tuples of edges. Only
$O_{r,k}(n^{k-1})$ of them contain two edges with a common
endpoint, given that $m=O_r(n)$.

A fixed $k$-matching is contained in $\Pi$ with probability $(n-k)!/n!=n^{-k}-O_k(n^{-k-1})$.
                                  
Consequently, Bonferroni's inequalities applied to \eqref{eq:rook} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:avoid-union}
 \Pr(\Pi\cap F_J=\varnothing)=\mathrm e^{-m/n}+o(1).
\end{equation}
Indeed, truncate inclusion--exclusion after $K$
terms.  Each truncated sum differs from the corresponding truncation of
$\exp(-m/n)$ by $O_{r,K}(n^{-1})$, while the two adjacent Bonferroni
bounds differ by at most
\[
        \frac{r^{K+1}}{(K+1)!}+O_{r,K}(n^{-1}).
\]
First let $K\to\infty$ and then $n\to\infty$.
Inclusion--exclusion over the events
$\{\Pi\cap M_i=\varnothing\}$ using \eqref{eq:avoid-union} gives that $\Pr\big(\Pi\cap M_i\ne\varnothing\text{ for every }i\in[r]\big) $ equals 
\[
 \sum_{J\subseteq[r]}(-1)^{|J|}\mathrm e^{-|F_J|/n}+o(1)=\prod_{i=1}^r \left(1- e^{-|M_i|/n}\right)+o(1)
   \leqslant (1-e^{-1})^r+o(1).          
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a row permutation $\pi\in\mathcal S_n$ uniformly at random, viewing it as
the perfect matching $\{(i,\pi(i)):i\in[n]\}$.  Define a
bipartite graph $B=B(\pi)$ whose two vertex classes are copies of $[n]$,
representing respectively the symbols of $L$ on the left and those of $P$ on the right.  Join $x$ to
$s$ if some filled cell $(i,j)$ of $P$ satisfies
\[
       L(\pi(i),j)=x
       \quad\text{and}\quad
       P(i,j)=s.                                                \tag{4}
\]
A perfect matching in the bipartite complement $\overline B$ pairs each
$L$-symbol $x$ with a $P$-symbol $s$ to which it is not adjacent.  Defining
$\sigma(x)=s$ gives precisely a symbol permutation for which
$\sigma(L(\pi(i),j))\ne P(i,j)$ in every filled cell.  We will show that some
choice of $\pi$ makes $\overline B$ have a perfect matching.

Set
\[
                 a=1-\mathrm e^{-1}.
\]
Suppose that the symbol $s$ occurs in $P$ at
$(i_1,j_1),\dots,(i_d,j_d)$.  These row indices and these column indices are
all distinct.  For a symbol $x$ of $L$, let $u_k$ be the unique row for which
$L(u_k,j_k)=x$, and put
\[
             M_{s,x}=\{(i_k,u_k):1\leqslant k\leqslant d\}.
\]
This is a matching: the $i_k$ are distinct, and an equality $u_k=u_\ell$ would
put $x$ twice in one row of $L$, since $j_k\ne j_\ell$.  Moreover, (4) says
exactly that
\[
               xs\in E(B)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
               \pi\cap M_{s,x}\ne\varnothing.                 \tag{5}
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:hit}
with $r=1$ gives, uniformly in $s$ and $x$,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E\deg_B(s)
   &=\sum_x\Pr(\pi\cap M_{s,x}\ne\varnothing)
     \leqslant (a+o(1))n,\\
 \mathbb E\deg_B(x)
   &=\sum_s\Pr(\pi\cap M_{s,x}\ne\varnothing)
     \leqslant (a+o(1))n.
\end{align*}
Thus
\[
               \mathbb E\deg_B(v)\leqslant (a+o(1))n                \tag{6}
\]
for every vertex $v$ in $B$.

Next fix three distinct symbols $x_1,x_2,x_3$ of $L$.  For each $s$, the
matchings $M_{s,x_1}$, $M_{s,x_2}$ and $M_{s,x_3}$ are pairwise
edge-disjoint.
Indeed, a common edge would, by its first coordinate, arise from the same
cell of $P$, and its second coordinate would then give
$x_i=x_j$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:hit}, now with $r=3$, yields
\[
 \mathbb E\bigl|N_B(x_1)\cap N_B(x_2)\cap N_B(x_3)\bigr|
   \leqslant (a^3+o(1))n.                                            \tag{7}
\]

Here and in (6), the $o(1)$ is uniform, as required when summing over the
symbols.

Interchanging two values of $\pi$ affects only two rows.  For a fixed
$P$-symbol, each affected row contains it at most once; for a fixed
$L$-symbol, each old or new row of $L$ contains it in exactly one column.
Thus the neighbourhood of any fixed vertex of $B$ changes in at most four
vertices.  A fixed degree is therefore $4$-Lipschitz under transpositions,
and a fixed triple common-neighbourhood size is $12$-Lipschitz.
For $n$ large, (3) followed by a union bound over the $2n$ degrees and fewer
than $n^3$ triples, shows that for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$ there is a choice of
$\pi$ for which 
\begin{align}
 \Delta(B)&\leqslant(a+\varepsilon)n\quad\text{and},                              \tag{8}\\
 |N_B(x_1)\cap N_B(x_2)\cap N_B(x_3)|
     &\leqslant(a^3+\varepsilon)n                                    \tag{9}
\end{align}
simultaneously for all distinct $x_1,x_2,x_3$.

Choose $\varepsilon>0$ small enough that
\[
                  a^3+\varepsilon<1-a-\varepsilon;             \tag{10}
\]
this is possible because
$ 
       (1-\mathrm e^{-1})^3<\mathrm e^{-1}$.
Fix a row permutation satisfying (8) and (9).  If $\overline B$ had no
perfect matching, Hall's theorem would give a set $X$ in its left class with
$|N_{\overline B}(X)|<|X|$.  Taking $Y=\cap_{x\in X}N_B(x)$ to be  
the complement of $N_{\overline B}(X)$  
in the right class, we obtain
\[
    X\times Y\subseteq E(B)
    \quad\text{and}\quad |X|+|Y|>n.              \tag{11}
\]
By (8), both $|X|$ and $|Y|$ are at most $(a+\varepsilon)n$; hence (11) gives
\[
    \min(|X|,|Y|)>(1-a-\varepsilon)n.                  \tag{12}
\]
For large $n$, we can choose three distinct vertices $x_1,x_2,x_3\in X$. Then (12), the definition of $Y$ and
(9) together imply
\[
 (1-a-\varepsilon)n
   <|Y|
   \leqslant |N_B(x_1)\cap N_B(x_2)\cap N_B(x_3)|
   \leqslant(a^3+\varepsilon)n,
\]
a contradiction of (10).  Thus $\overline B$ has a perfect matching.  As observed
above, its matching map is the required symbol permutation $\sigma$.

name: Proof of \tref{thm:main

label: cj:alln
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{cj:alln}
    If $L$ and $L'$ are any Latin squares of the same order $n>1$, then there is a principal isotope of $L'$ that avoids $L$.
head: environment

label: cj:genACM
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{cj:genACM}
For any constant $t$ 
the following is true for every sufficiently large integers $n$. Suppose that $L$ is a Latin square of order $n$. 
Suppose that $A$ is an $n\times n$ array of subsets of $[n]$, each of size at most $t$, in which
each symbol occurs at most $t$ times among the sets in each row and column. Then there is a principal isotope of $L$ that avoids $A$.
head: environment
